_comment: The two alarms design.md 12.6 says are worth having on day one. Alarms are configuration, not console state, for the same reasons the guardrail is (design.md 10.1): reviewable in a pull request, diffable, reproducible in another account. Apply with scripts/apply_alarms.py.
_naming: Every name carries the -dev suffix so generated resources can coexist with manually created ones during the migration to IaC (design.md 11, point 2).

notification._note: Alarms point here. An alarm with no action is not an alarm, so apply_alarms.py refuses to create one without a topic, and warns when the topic it created has no subscribers — an alarm nobody is subscribed to fails the same way one paragraph further out.
notification._subscriptions: Deliberately not declared here. SNS email subscriptions require the recipient to confirm out of band, so a config file cannot make one true; subscribe once, by hand, and the script tells you if you have not.

metric_filters.name: grocery-orchestrator-handler-escaped-dev
metric_filters._pattern_note: A JSON selector, NOT the substring "handler_escaped". A substring pattern matches any log line that happens to contain the text — an exception message quoting it, a test fixture, a future log line about the alarm itself — and each of those is a page at 3am for nothing. This binds to the structured field Powertools writes.
metric_filters._default_value_note: 0, not absent. Without it the metric has datapoints only when the pattern matches, so the alarm sits in INSUFFICIENT_DATA forever and OK never means 'checked and fine' — it means 'never looked'. With 0-fill, a quiet period is an affirmative all-clear.

metric_filters.name: grocery-ingestion-row-rejected-dev
metric_filters._why: The ingestion Lambda REFUSES a row whose unit price is implausible against its own pack size -- the $2,490-broccoli class, which reached the live products table once and was invisible because a diff reports change and a defect on a FIRST write is not a change. A refused row is dropped rather than corrected, so without this metric the only trace is a count in a Step Functions execution nobody reads on a good day.
metric_filters._pattern_note: A JSON selector on the structured field ingestion/handler.py::_log_rejection writes, for the same reason the handler-escaped filter is: a substring pattern would also match this comment quoted in an exception, a test fixture, or a future log line about the alarm itself.
metric_filters._no_powertools_note: The ingestion Lambda prints the line as plain JSON rather than through Powertools. AGENTS.md forbids importing aws_lambda_powertools outside src/handler.py and src/observability/powertools.py, because that import is what would end the no-AWS property CI depends on -- and tests/test_ingestion.py runs this module with no account. A metric filter needs no library at either end.

metric_filters.name: grocery-ingestion-history-write-failed-dev
metric_filters._why: The price-history append failed while the products write succeeded. ingestion/handler.py::_append_history DEGRADES rather than failing the refresh -- history is ops/reviewer bookkeeping, never on the shopper path, and failing a branch whose actual job was done would report a working refresh as a broken one. A degradation nobody can see is the failure this repository keeps finding, so the degradation is metered here.
metric_filters._not_the_same_as_the_execution_alarm: grocery-ingestion-refresh-failed-dev catches a refresh that THREW. This one catches a refresh that SUCCEEDED with its history missing. Two different facts, two alarms.
metric_filters._pattern_note: A JSON selector on the structured field _append_history writes, for the same reason the rejection and handler-escaped filters use one: a substring pattern would also match this text quoted in an exception or a future log line about the alarm itself.

metric_filters.name: grocery-ingestion-refresh-failed-dev
metric_filters._why: One retailer's refresh threw. Products may not have been written at all, so this is the ingestion failure with a shopper-visible consequence: prices for that chain age one more day toward STALE_DATA with nothing saying why. The line names the exception class and its first 300 characters, so the common causes -- AccessDenied on a table or a grant that was never applied, a source that refused, the fixture guard refusing to shadow the real catalogue -- are distinguishable without opening an execution.
metric_filters._why_the_state_machine_alarm_cannot_see_: grocery-ingestion-failed-dev watches AWS/States ExecutionsFailed, and a thrown branch does not fail the execution. config/ingestion-state-machine.json catches States.ALL INSIDE the item processor and routes it to a Pass state, precisely so a broken Pak'nSave does not discard a good New World refresh -- so the execution SUCCEEDS with one branch marked failed, and the state-machine failure metric correctly reports nothing. That is the right state machine and the wrong place to watch from. A per-branch failure exists as an observable fact only in the Lambda's own log, which is where this filter reads it.
metric_filters._pattern_note: A JSON selector on the structured field ingestion/handler.py::_log_refresh_failure writes, for the same reason every other filter here uses one: a substring pattern would also match this text quoted in an exception or a future log line about the alarm itself.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-handler-escaped-dev
alarms.description: An exception escaped every handler in src/handler.py and hit the last resort in lambda_handler(). Always a bug: every anticipated failure is mapped to an error event before this point. The log line carries the exception type and file:line frames.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-api-5xx-dev
alarms.description: Any 5xx from the API. The gateway's own metric, so it fires even when the failure is upstream of our code or logging is the thing that broke — which is why it overlaps the handler_escaped alarm deliberately.
alarms._dimensions_note: ApiName must match the deployed API exactly. A dimension that matches nothing yields a metric with no datapoints, which looks identical to a healthy service.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-internal-error-dev
alarms.description: The turn failed for a reason the handler could not attribute -- INTERNAL_ERROR, as distinct from an honest refusal. THIS IS THE ALARM THAT WAS MISSING, and its absence was found on 2026-08-30: a production stage missing USE_DYNAMODB or a guardrail version raises ConfigurationError, which maps to a contract-valid INTERNAL_ERROR at HTTP 200. That fires neither handler-escaped (it logs unhandled_exception, not handler_escaped) nor api-5xx (it is a 200). The most consequential failure the service has was invisible to both deployed alarms. Dimensioned on code so an honest BUDGET_INFEASIBLE or NO_DATA never pages anyone.
alarms._threshold_note: Three in five minutes, not one. A single INTERNAL_ERROR is a transient upstream fault the client retries; a misconfiguration produces one on EVERY turn, so it crosses three almost immediately. The gap between those is what stops this being the alarm people mute.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-idempotency-unavailable-dev
alarms.description: The idempotency store could not be reached. The turn still runs -- degrading to work rather than failing is deliberate (Req 12.3.4) -- so nothing else reports it and a client timeout retry is now charged twice. Silent double-billing is the failure this makes visible.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-turn-latency-dev
alarms.description: p95 turn latency against the 20-second meal-plan target in the pilot acceptance criteria (Req 12.6). Extended statistic rather than Average: an average hides the tail, and the tail is what the 29-second gateway ceiling truncates.
alarms._threshold_note: Milliseconds. Two consecutive periods, because one slow five minutes on a service doing single-figure turns per minute is one slow request, not a trend.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-repair-exhausted-dev
alarms.description: The bounded repair loop ran out of attempts and the plan was discarded. Each one is an honest refusal the shopper sees, so a trickle is the system working; a cluster means the planner is producing drafts that cannot be validated -- a prompt regression, a model change, or a catalogue whose candidates no longer satisfy the constraints.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-guardrail-interventions-dev
alarms.description: A spike in Guardrail interventions. NOT a safety alarm -- an intervention is the control working, and alarming on one would page somebody every time the policy did its job. It is a CHANGE detector, and it exists because of a real incident: the deployed function applied Guardrail version 1 for days while every document described version 2, and benign grocery queries were refused with nothing to show for it. A policy or version change that starts over-blocking looks exactly like this.

alarms.name: grocery-orchestrator-silent-turns-dev
alarms.description: Turns that produced no content -- no comparison, no plan, no clarification. Dimensioned by intent, so a rise on meal_plan is distinguishable from a rise on out_of_scope. A shopper who asks and is answered with nothing has had a worse experience than one who was refused, and no other signal reports it: the turn is a 200 with a contract-valid body.

alarms.name: grocery-ingestion-failed-dev
alarms.description: THE NIGHTLY REFRESH FAILED AS A WHOLE. The Step Functions execution metric, not one we publish, so it fires even when the failure is upstream of our code, before our logging runs, or IS our logging -- the same reasoning as the API 5xx alarm. What reaches it is a failure of the EXECUTION: a malformed input (no $.retailers), a state-machine definition bug, a Map that could not run, a Catch that could not apply. Check the execution history: aws stepfunctions list-executions --status-filter FAILED.
alarms._what_it_does_not_cover_and_why: A single retailer's branch throwing does NOT fail the execution, so it does not reach this alarm. config/ingestion-state-machine.json catches States.ALL inside the item processor and routes it to a Pass state -- deliberately, so one broken retailer does not discard the two that succeeded -- and the execution then reports SUCCEEDED with that branch marked failed. This was recorded wrongly when the alarm was added on 2026-09-03: it was described as catching 'a refresh that THREW', which is the one thing the Catch guarantees it cannot see. grocery-ingestion-refresh-failed-dev covers the branch case, from the Lambda's own log, because that is the only place a caught failure still exists.
alarms._why_row_rejected_was_not_enough: grocery-ingestion-row-rejected-dev counts REJECTED ROWS. A branch that THROWS never reaches the rejection counter, so it emits no datapoint at all -- and treat_missing_data notBreaching correctly reads no datapoints as healthy. An alarm on the work product cannot see the work not happening. That gap made a real defect silent: on 2026-09-02 the price-history write shipped without its table or its IAM grant (acc53fb), so a scheduled refresh would write products and then fail on AccessDenied, every night, visible only to somebody who opened the execution history. The alarm that actually closes that gap is grocery-ingestion-refresh-failed-dev, not this one.
alarms._dimensions_note: StateMachineArn must match the deployed state machine exactly. Placeholders are resolved from STS at apply time like every other ARN here; a dimension that matches nothing yields a metric with no datapoints, which looks identical to a healthy service.
alarms._period_note: An hour, matching the row-rejected alarm and for the same reason: the refresh is a DAILY schedule, so a five-minute window is mostly empty by construction and the signal would depend on which window the run landed in.
alarms._threshold_note: One. There is no volume at which a failed daily refresh is normal.

alarms.name: grocery-ingestion-row-rejected-dev
alarms.description: Ingestion refused at least one row as implausible. NOT an outage: the row was dropped, the previous good row survives and will age into STALE_DATA, and the shopper sees an honest gap rather than a wrong price. It means the normaliser, the source data, or a pack size changed -- run `python scripts/check_ingestion_anomalies.py` and read the rejected sample in the Step Functions execution.
alarms._threshold_note: One row, not a percentage. The original defect hit six rows out of 2,759 (0.2%), so any percentage gate loose enough to tolerate a real special would have slept straight through it. Verified 2026-08-31 by reintroducing the defect: 522 of 2,759 rows would have been refused against the REAL catalogue, because 19% of it is sold-each. The six was an artefact of the seeded fixture set, not the size of the class.
alarms._period_note: An hour, not the five minutes the request-path alarms use. The refresh is a DAILY schedule, so a five-minute window is mostly empty by construction and the signal would depend on which window the run landed in.

alarms.name: grocery-ingestion-history-write-failed-dev
alarms.description: The nightly refresh wrote prices but could not append price history. NOT an outage and not shopper-visible: the products table is current, and history is the data-quality reviewer's baseline (src/history). What it costs is a sample -- and a baseline with gaps answers 'this price doubled overnight' less well every time this fires. Check the table exists and the ingestion role still grants PutItem/BatchWriteItem on it; the log line names the error class.
alarms._period_note: An hour, matching the other ingestion alarms: the refresh is daily.
alarms._threshold_note: One. The refresh runs once a day over three retailers, so a single failure is a third of a day's history missing, not noise.

alarms.name: grocery-ingestion-refresh-failed-dev
alarms.description: ONE RETAILER'S REFRESH THREW, and the execution reported success anyway. That is by design -- the Map catches per-branch failures so the retailers that worked are not discarded -- which is exactly why this alarm is needed: without it the failure exists only as a status field in an execution nobody reads on a good day. The prices for that chain were not refreshed. Read the log line: it names the exception class and the first 300 characters of the message.
alarms._why_it_reads_the_log_and_not_the_state_: AWS/States ExecutionsFailed cannot see a caught branch (grocery-ingestion-failed-dev says so at length). A Lambda that raises still writes this line first, so the fact survives the Catch that is about to hide it.
alarms._period_note: An hour, matching the other ingestion alarms: the refresh is daily, so a five-minute window is empty by construction.
alarms._threshold_note: One. Three retailers refresh once a day; one of them failing is a third of the catalogue not refreshed, and there is no volume at which that is routine.

_coverage_note: Req 12.8 asks for escaped handlers and API 5xx before pilot traffic, then MEASURED alarms for latency, model errors, Guardrail interventions, throttling, stale data, idempotency failures and silent turns. The first two shipped 2026-08-27; the rest were added 2026-08-30 after an audit found that the most consequential failure the service has -- a production stage silently configured as a demo -- fired neither of them. Every alarm here binds to a metric CONFIRMED present in CloudWatch with the dimensions named, because an alarm on a metric that never reports looks exactly like a healthy service. Still absent deliberately: throttling and stale-data alarms, because neither has a metric yet -- adding the alarm before the metric would be adding the appearance of coverage.
_emf_note: Metrics the APPLICATION emits as Embedded Metric Format, as distinct from metric_filters, which CloudWatch derives from log lines. Both end up in the same namespace and an alarm can watch either, but only filters are declared by this file -- so EMF names are listed here explicitly rather than left unvalidated. That keeps the teeth: an alarm on a mistyped metric name still fails validation, and a metric name that never reports looks exactly like a healthy service. tests/test_alarms.py asserts this list matches the METRIC_ constants in src/observability/base.py, so renaming a metric in code without updating an alarm fails the build.
